paper_title: Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to jointly localize a target in space and time given a natural-language query. Despite continued advances, existing STVG benchmarks remain largely centered on localizing targets through instance-specific descriptions, leaving them largely decoupled from long-form reasoning increasingly emphasized in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In this paper, we introduce Event-STVG, a task that shifts STVG from locating what is described toward event-level reasoning by unifying long-form context, repeated-event reasoning, event localization, role inference, and multi-target grounding. To facilitate research on Event-STVG, we construct a large-scale benchmark comprising 4,016 annotated event occurrences across soccer and seven additional domains. Experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal substantial difficulty, with the strongest model achieving only 5.4% m-vIoU at the 10-minute horizon. Across domains, we consistently observe confusion among repeated same-type events, spatial grounding bottlenecks, and rare success in jointly grounding all required roles. Event-STVG establishes a new challenge for visual understanding in MLLMs, calling for future models that can jointly reason about complex events across space and time. Code and annotations are available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/EventSTVG

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to jointly localize target of interest in space and time within an untrimmed video given natural-language query (Zhang et al., 2020). By linking natural-language queries to precise spatiotemporal localization in video, STVG provides concrete means of evaluating fine-grained multimodal grounding. Research in this area has advanced both grounding methods (Yang et al., 2022; Rasheed et al., 2026) and task formulations, with recent work extending STVG to multiple targets (Yao et al., 2026), long-form videos (Gu et al., 2026), and compositional queries (Wang et al., 2026b). Despite their growing complexity, existing STVG tasks remain largely centered on descriptionguided localization. For example, the query in Figure 2 identifies woman through her appearance, 1 Figure 2: Comparison between Event-STVG and existing STVG. Existing STVG primarily performs description-guided localization, whereas Event-STVG requires complex event-level reasoning. action, and relation to another person. As result, current STVG benchmarks primarily test whether models can match detailed linguistic description to the corresponding visual instance. This formulation is well suited to precise referent localization, but places limited demands on the richer long-form reasoning capabilities increasingly expected of MLLMs. To move STVG beyond description-guided localization, we introduce Event-STVG, new formulation that turns spatio-temporal grounding into test of long-form event reasoning in MLLMs. Rather than describing the target instance directly, Event-STVG specifies an event category, its ordinal occurrence, and set of semantic roles, requiring models to resolve the target occurrence, infer the corresponding role fillers, and jointly ground the event interval and its participants. This brings STVG substantially closer to the long-context temporal reasoning, repeated-event disambiguation, structured role inference, and multi-entity grounding increasingly emphasized in recent MLLM benchmarks (Cheng et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Aparcedo et al., 2026; Asgarov et al., 2026). To study this formulation at scale, we construct the accompanying benchmark, also named Event-STVG, comprising 4,016 annotated event occurrences spanning 8 domains, 26 event types, and 30 semantic roles. We use soccer as the primary domain because of its visually similar players, consistent scenes, and multi-participant interactions. Specifically, 3,516 soccer events in the 1-minute setting support broad evaluation across models, while 300-event subsets at 3, 5, and 10 minutes enable controlled analysis of how performance changes with increasing temporal context. The remaining 500 events span seven additional domains and are organized into 100 minute-scale, multi-occurrence challenges, allowing us to examine whether the observed difficulties generalize beyond soccer. Comprehensive experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs and specialized STVG model reveal that Event-STVG remains highly challenging. The strongest model achieves only 5.4% vIoU with 10-minute context. More importantly, our analyses reveal several recurring bottlenecks across frontier models. As context grows, models increasingly confuse the requested occurrence with other same-type events. Even when the target event is successfully localized, performance deteriorates sharply under role-grounding evaluation. Moreover, models rarely ground all required roles correctly within the same event. These findings expose persistent gap between resolving when an event occurs and grounding the structured participants that constitute it. Our main contributions are threefold: (1) We rethink what STVG should evaluate for MLLMs and introduce Event-STVG, task reframing spatio-temporal grounding from description-guided localization toward test of long-form event reasoning in MLLMs. (2) We construct high-quality benchmark, also named Event-STVG, comprising 4,016 annotated event occurrences across 8 domains, and comprehensively evaluate frontier MLLMs together with specialized STVG model, revealing substantial challenges in joint spatio-temporal grounding. 2 (3) We conduct systematic error analyses across models and domains, identifying consistent failure patterns in event-instance selection, spatial role grounding, and complete event grounding. These findings provide insights for improving both general-purpose MLLMs and STVG specialists.

Meanwhile, benchmark extensions to STVG address multiple targets (Ji et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2026), compositional queries (Wang et al., 2026b), specialized domains (Otsubo et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2025), and minute-scale contexts (Gu et al., 2026). Yet these formulations remain largely description-guided, with instance-specific appearance, action, or relational cues specifying what should be grounded. Existing STVG therefore primarily evaluates description-conditioned detection and localization rather than more complex event-level reasoning in MLLMs. Structured and Grounded Event Understanding Event understanding has long been modeled through predicates, semantic roles, and visual grounding, from imSitu to CineMEC (Yatskar et al., 2016; Pratt et al., 2020; Sadhu et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2022; Darur et al., 2026). These formulations operate on images or pre-segmented short events and thus do not require event temporal grounding. VidEvent and NEST introduce event localization and structured argument understanding but do not spatially ground role fillers (Liang et al., 2025; Asgarov et al., 2026); MultiVENT-G additionally grounds role-specific spatial evidence but separates temporal and spatial retrieval (Sanders et al., 2024). To our knowledge, no prior benchmark jointly requires temporal grounding of target event and spatial grounding of its constituent semantic-role fillers. Video QA with Spatio-Temporal Evidence General video QA benchmarks primarily evaluate answer correctness (Fu et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), while recent benchmarks increasingly require visual evidence through temporal localization (Chen et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) or decomposed spatio-temporal grounding (Deng et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026). More recently, E-VQA jointly grounds objects or regions supporting an answer (Wang et al., 2026a), while CaST-Bench localizes evidence along causal reasoning chain (Zhang et al., 2026a). These benchmarks ground evidence supporting an answer or reasoning process, rather than jointly localizing an event and the semantic-role fillers that constitute its structure. 3 Figure 3: Overview of Event-STVG benchmark construction and composition. We construct EventSTVG through carefully designed human annotation with automated tracking assistance and multistage quality control. The resulting benchmark exhibits substantial diversity in event types and semantic roles, covering major soccer events and seven additional domains.

sections.title: 3 EVENT-STVG
sections.content: 3.1 TASK FORMULATION Distinct from prior formulations, Event-STVG jointly requires temporal localization of the specified event occurrence and spatial grounding of its constituent roles, testing eventrole reasoning in longform video. The task can be formulated as follows. Given long-form video , an event type may occur repeatedly, forming an ordered sequence of event instances Each event type is associated with semantic role schema E(V, E) = E1, E2, . . . , En. R(E) = {r1, r2, . . . , rK}, which specifies the constituent roles involved in the event. Given an event type E, an ordinal index m, and set of required roles Rq R(E), Event-STVG asks model to identify the m-th occurrence Em and jointly return its temporal interval m, te m] τm = [ts together with the spatial trajectory of each queried role within that interval, Bm = {Bm,r Rq}, where Bm,r denotes the sequence of bounding boxes grounding the entity that fills role r. Thus, the query specifies what event, which occurrence, and which roles, but provides no instance-specific description of the participants, their appearance, or how the event unfolds. To reduce ambiguity in annotation and evaluation, we define event-specific temporal boundaries using canonical role actions, specifying only when an event begins and ends rather than how its constituent roles interact. For example, soccer shot may be defined from possession by the last passer to the point at which the shot outcome becomes clear. Different occurrences may nevertheless realize the same event structure differently, such as through cross followed by header or through ball followed by shot. These instance-specific interaction patterns are neither encoded in the query nor prescribed by the event definition, and must therefore be inferred from the video to resolve the target occurrence and ground its constituent roles.

sections.title: 3.2 BENCHMARK CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: Data Sources and Scope Under this formulation, Event-STVG naturally applies to diverse realworld scenarios in which events recur over time with shared role structures but different participants and realizations. Examples include grounding the participants in particular restaurant order, the entities in specific traffic accident, or the part produced in given manufacturing cycle. Considering both the availability of existing video datasets and our emphasis on structured multi-participant activities, we instantiate our benchmark primarily with soccer, complemented by basketball, volleyball, ice hockey, animal hunting, fast-food packing, entertainment programs, and esports as shown in Figure 3. The videos are drawn from SoccerNet-v2 (Deli`ege et al., 2021), PL-NBA (Zhao et al., 2026), VNL-STES (Nguyen et al., 2025), VIP-HTD (Prakash et al., 2024), MammalNet (Chen et al., 2023), and publicly available YouTube videos. Human Annotation The annotation of soccer follows the process illustrated in Figure 3. We first use SoccerNet-v2 event annotations to automatically retrieve candidate occurrences. Annotators then inspect each candidate segment and manually determine its start and end according to eventspecific boundary definitions. To annotate role trajectories efficiently, we use SoccerMaster (Yang et al., 2026) together with tracking and re-identification tools to generate candidate detections and track identities, which are presented to annotators at 2 FPS. Annotators bind tracks to event-specific semantic roles such as shooter, last passer, and goalkeeper, while retaining full control to reassign tracks, remove erroneous boxes, or manually add missing boxes. Thus, automatic tracking serves only as annotation assistance, while all ground-truth trajectories are human-verified. Starting from these annotations, we construct evaluation contexts ranging from oracle event windows to contexts of up to 10 minutes. Occurrences of each event type are temporally ordered within each context to derive ordinal indices, after which Event-STVG queries are generated from the event type, ordinal index, and required roles. For the remaining domains, since source annotations and tracking availability vary across domains, we use source-agnostic human annotation procedure. Annotators manually determine event boundaries and ground semantic roles either by assigning available tracking boxes or by manually drawing boxes on video frames sampled at 2 FPS. This yields 500 events with temporal intervals and role trajectories. We organize them into 100 minute-scale evaluation videos by extracting continuous intervals from source videos when possible or, otherwise, concatenating related clips from the same game or from videos of the same animal species. Repeated events are then enumerated to construct ordinal event-role queries following the task formulation. Quality Control We independently cross-annotate approximately 10% of the data for both temporal segmentation and role grounding. The paired annotations achieve mean temporal IoU of 0.9039 for event intervals and mean spatial IoU of 0.9161 when averaged equally over samplerole pairs. We further sample approximately 5% of the data and inspect the corresponding annotations to verify the correctness of ordinal indices and generated prompts, with all the inspected annotations passing the checks. Appendix provides further details on annotation and quality control.

sections.title: 3.3 BENCHMARK STATISTICS
sections.content: As shown in Figure 3, our benchmark comprises 4,016 annotated event instances across soccer and seven additional domains. Together, they contain 26 event types, 30 semantic roles, 7,323 eventrole pairs and 59,381 annotated bounding boxes, providing dense temporal and spatial supervision for event occurrence selection and role grounding. Notably, 58.91% of all event instances involve multiple semantic roles, making the joint grounding of multiple role fillers common requirement. Ordinal disambiguation is also central to Event-STVG. The proportion of soccer contexts containing repeated same-type events increases from 13.68% at one minute to 68.69% at ten minutes, while 99.40% of queries in the remaining domains contain repeated same-type occurrences.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENT
sections.content: 4.1 SETTINGS Evaluated Models We evaluate ten vision-language models, including nine general-purpose VLMs and one STVG specialist: Gemini-3.7 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026), GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026), Qwen-3.8 Max (Qwen Team, 2026c), Qwen-3.7 Plus (Qwen Team, 2026b), Qwen-3.5 9B (Qwen Team, 2026a), GLM-5.3 Flash (Z.ai, 2026), GLM-5V Turbo (GLM-V Team, 2026), 5 GLM-4.6V (GLM-V Team, 2025), MiniMax-M3 (Lai et al., 2026), and PTD with its released Qwen3-VL-4B checkpoint (Rasheed et al., 2026). This selection spans leading proprietary models, open-weight models, locally deployable models, and task-specialized STVG model. Evaluation Protocol For soccer, we evaluate all 3,516 events under the oracle and 1-minute settings. Under the oracle setting, models are given the ground-truth event interval and evaluated only on role grounding, isolating spatial grounding from temporal retrieval. These oracle windows are therefore not counted as complete Event-STVG videos in Table 1. Building on the 1-minute setting, which provides the primary short-context evaluation of end-to-end Event-STVG, we further evaluate fixed stratified subset of 300 events under each of the 3-, 5-, and 10-minute settings to assess long-context robustness. Finally, 100 cross-domain evaluation videos assess generalization beyond soccer. In total, this gives 4,516 non-oracle evaluation videos across the benchmark. Prompt templates and model evaluation details are provided in Appendices and C, respectively. Metrics We report mean temporal IoU (m-tIoU) (Zhang et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022) for event intervals and mean video IoU (m-vIoU) for role trajectories. Event-level vIoU (Zhang et al., 2020) averages tube IoU over queried roles; m-vIoU then averages over events. We also report vIoU@0.3 and vIoU@0.5, the proportions of events above each event-level threshold. Missing or invalid predictions contribute zero. The consistently low performance across team-sport domains further positions soccer as representative and demanding main testbed for structured event grounding. 4.3 ERROR ANALYSIS We analyze the low performance of end-to-end grounding through three hierarchical bottlenecks: (1) event-instance resolution, where the model must distinguish the queried occurrence from other instances of the same event type; (2) spatial role grounding, where the model must correctly localize the semantic role fillers after identifying the event temporally; and (3) multi-role composition, where the model must jointly ground all required role fillers to recover the complete event structure. These bottlenecks form increasingly demanding levels of Event-STVG, from resolving the target event occurrence, to grounding its constituent roles, and finally to composing them into complete eventlevel evidence. The first bottleneck is particularly pronounced in sports scenes with repeated sametype events, while the latter two remain prominent across domains. Bottleneck I: Resolving the target occurrence among repeated events Longer inputs primarily impair event-instance resolution rather than boundary localization after the target occurrence has been identified in soccer videos. As the input becomes longer, models increasingly select another valid occurrence of the same event type instead of the annotated target. Correspondingly, target hit rates decrease and instance-confusion rates increase significantly for all three models when sametype distractors are present (all Holm-adjusted < 0.0001). sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we introduce Event-STVG, new formulation of spatio-temporal video grounding that shifts description-guided localization toward structured event reasoning. To this end, we construct benchmark with 4,016 manually annotated event occurrences across eight domains, which requires models to resolve target occurrence among repeated events, infer its semantic role fillers, and jointly ground them in space and time. Our experiments show that current models remain far from solving Event-STVG, with the best model achieving only 5.4% m-vIoU under 10-minute context. The analyses further reveal three key challenges: (1) longer contexts hinder event-instance resolution, especially with repeated same-type events; (2) temporal localization does not ensure accurate spatial role grounding; and (3) complete grounding becomes substantially harder with multiple semantic roles. Event-STVG thus moves beyond viewing MLLMs merely as multimodal alignment tools toward evaluating the deeper reasoning required for structured event understanding. More broadly, its verifiable grounding signals may also provide fine-grained feedback for reinforcement learningbased post-training toward stronger visual reasoning. We hope Event-STVG can serve as testbed for advancing long-form event reasoning through verifiable spatio-temporal grounding. sections.title: B PROMPT TEMPLATES AND OUTPUT FORMAT
sections.content: We query each model with an event type, an ordinal occurrence, event-specific temporal boundaries, and the roles to ground. The following is the prompt template for 10-minute soccer video and the Shot on Target event. The ordinal placeholder is replaced by the requested occurrence index. You will see 10-minute soccer match video. Find the {ordinal} occurrence of Shot on Target. The event starts when the last passer first gains possession during the target attack, and ends when the outcome of the shot becomes clear. Draw bounding boxes for the last passer, the shooter, and the defending goalkeeper. Instructions: Report the events start and end times in seconds relative to the input video. Starting at the events start time, provide role boxes every 0.5 seconds within the event window. For each sampled timestamp, include all three roles: last passer, shooter, and goalkeeper. Use tight bounding boxes in [xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax] format, normalized to [0, 1000], with the origin at the top-left of the frame. Track the same person for each role throughout the event. If that person is not reliably visible, output null; resume tracking the same person when visible again. Return only JSON with temporal window (start sec, role localization (time sec and each roles box or null). end sec) and The required output is JSON object with one temporal window and list of role localizations. sections.title: C EVALUATION PROTOCOL AND IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: This appendix provides additional details on the evaluation protocol, model input configurations, failure handling, and supplementary experiments used in Event-STVG. Unless otherwise stated, all metrics are reported as percentages. For paired comparisons, we use 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples with fixed seed of 21 and report two-sided 95% percentile confidence intervals. C.1 EVALUATION SETTINGS Soccer benchmark. The main soccer benchmark contains 3,516 target event queries with 6,497 required role instances. The Oracle and 1-minute settings use the same target events. In the Oracle setting, the model is directly given the ground-truth event clip and is evaluated only on grounding the required semantic roles, thereby isolating spatial role grounding from temporal event retrieval. In the 1-minute setting, the model receives frozen one-minute context and must identify the queried occurrence according to its ordinal index, predict the event interval, and ground all required role fillers. For the long-context evaluation, we use fixed stratified subset of 300 target events and evaluate the same targets under 3-, 5-, and 10-minute contexts. Because enlarging the temporal context may introduce additional occurrences of the same event type, ordinal indices are recomputed independently for each context duration. The corresponding frozen query for each duration is used directly during inference. Multidomain evaluation. The multidomain extension contains 500 queries over 100 videos and is evaluated independently from the soccer benchmark. It uses the same Event-STVG formulation but domain-specific event and role definitions. Aggregation. The basic evaluation unit is query. For query requiring multiple semantic roles, role-level grounding scores are first averaged equally across the required roles, after which querylevel scores are averaged over the evaluation set. Different experimental subsets, such as the 300query long-context set and the supplementary robustness subsets described below, are therefore reported separately rather than pooled. C.2 MODEL INPUTS AND INFERENCE CONFIGURATION Different models expose different native video interfaces. We therefore follow each models supported interface while keeping the semantic task specification fixed whenever possible. The main configurations are summarized in Table C.1. Model / interface Video input Inference setting GPT-5.6 Sol Gemini-3.7 Flash (1 min) Qwen / GLM / MiniMax API models Native MP4 video input Native MP4 video input Qwen3.5-9B API baseline Uniformly sampled 64 frames PTD (Qwen3-VL-4B) 2 FPS JPEG frames, 512288, quality 80 2 FPS JPEG frames, 512288, quality 85 Google GenAI interface; provider generation defaults detail=low; provider generation defaults Provider generation defaults Fixed OpenRouter/SiliconFlow route; provider generation defaults FP16, SDPA, greedy decoding Table C.1: Main video input and inference protocols. Provider-native video models receive the original MP4 rather than client-side reconstruction of the 2 FPS frame sequence. For all hosted API models, optional generation parameters such as temperature, top-p, and random seed are left unspecified. Thus, provider defaults indicates that these values are determined by the serving platform and should not be interpreted as temperature = 0. The seed used for dataset sampling and bootstrap analysis is not sent to the models. For GPT-5.6 Sol, videos are converted to ordered JPEG frames at 2 FPS and 512288 resolution. The main soccer experiments use at most 1,200 frames, which covers the full 10-minute context at 2 FPS. The multidomain evaluation permits up to 1,300 frames to accommodate the longest videos. Each frame is accompanied by its corresponding timestamp. 17 All inference outputs are retained before parsing. Failed requests, malformed responses, and missing predictions remain part of the predefined evaluation set rather than being removed post hoc. C.3 PARSING AND SCORING RULES We use the same frozen parser and evaluator for all general-purpose models. response is considered parseable when unique complete JSON prediction can be extracted from the returned text. We allow single JSON object enclosed in code block or embedded in surrounding text, but do not repair malformed brackets, choose among multiple alternative answers, reorder coordinates, or clip invalid coordinates. valid bounding box must contain four finite values in xyxy order, lie within [0, 1000], and have positive width and height. valid predicted temporal interval must satisfy where is the duration of the input video. 0 ts te T, Importantly, temporal and spatial components are evaluated independently whenever possible. For example, prediction with valid temporal interval but missing role boxes can still receive nonzero temporal IoU while receiving zero spatial credit. Conversely, an invalid temporal interval receives zero temporal and joint spatio-temporal scores. This component-wise evaluation avoids discarding otherwise valid portions of partially structured predictions. Temporal IoU is computed between the predicted and ground-truth event intervals. For role grounding, the joint vIoU is computed over the union of the ground-truth and predicted temporal supports, such that missing boxes, spatial errors, and temporal over-extension are all penalized. Scores for multiple required roles are averaged equally within each query. Failed API requests and unparseable responses are assigned zero for the affected components and remain in the original evaluation denominator. We never select predictions according to their groundtruth score. C.4 REPEATABILITY UNDER DEFAULT INFERENCE SETTINGS Hosted API models may exhibit run-to-run variation even when the request configuration is unchanged. To quantify this effect, we sample fixed set of 352 soccer queries and repeat inference twice in addition to the original run. The same query IDs are used for Oracle and 1-minute evaluation. We perform this experiment for GLM-4.6V, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3.7-Plus, and Qwen3.8-Max. PTD is evaluated on the same subset as deterministic local reference. All values are percentages and failures remain in the denominator. The two Qwen models show relatively small Oracle variation, although their 1-minute results are not identical across runs. For example, Qwen3.8-Max changes from 47.726% to 44.702% m-tIoU between R0 and R2, corresponding to paired difference of 3.024 pp with 95% bootstrap interval of [5.600, 0.439]. 18 The larger variation of GLM-4.6V is primarily associated with service-side input failures rather than changes among successfully parsed predictions. Its Oracle runs contain 0, 135, and 152 API errors, respectively, with the additional failures reported as HTTP 400 image-input parsing errors. On the subset successfully parsed in all three runs, Oracle m-vIoU varies only from 12.521% to 13.439%. We therefore retain failures in the end-to-end statistics instead of interpreting the full-score decrease solely as stochastic decoding variation. PTD produces identical outputs across all three runs under the fixed 64-frame greedy configuration. This establishes repeatability for the evaluated configuration and subset. C.5 PTD BASELINE AND INTERFACE ADAPTATION PTD is designed around referring-object localization interface rather than the structured EventSTVG JSON interface. We therefore use its native inference format and convert the resulting specialtoken representation into the common Event-STVG evaluation format. For each semantic role, PTD receives role-specific referring expression derived only from the frozen event and role definition. For example, for shot-on-target event, the three role queries are: last passer: shooter before the shot the attacking player who makes the final effective pass to the shooter: the attacking player who takes the shot goalkeeper: the goalkeeper defending the goal against the shot Each role is inferred independently using the same 64 uniformly sampled video frames. Oracle clips containing fewer than 64 distinct source frames retain all available frames; otherwise, 64 frames are uniformly sampled. The model uses FP16 inference, SDPA attention, single GPU worker, maximum of 1,024 generated tokens, and greedy decoding. PTD time tokens denote sampled temporal positions rather than absolute seconds. We map these positions back to source-video time using the sampled frame indices and convert the sparse predicted boxes to the 0.5-second evaluation grid by interpolation only between valid neighboring predictions; no temporal extrapolation is performed. Failed roles are treated as missing roles rather than causing the complete query to be discarded. semantic difference remains between the native PTD interface and the full Event-STVG query. In particular, the PTD referring expression does not explicitly preserve the ordinal event index or the complete event-boundary specification, and multi-role queries are decomposed into independent role requests. This distinction is immaterial in the Oracle setting, where the target event has already been cropped, but can affect the 1-minute setting when several same-type events occur in the context. To quantify the effect of this interface adaptation, we additionally apply the PTD-style role-by-role query and output protocol to Qwen3.8-Max on the same fixed subset, as analyzed below. C.6 CONTROLLED COMPARISON WITH THE PTD-STYLE QUERY AND OUTPUT ADAPTATION On the same fixed, event-stratified subset of 100 Event-STVG queries, we compare three conditions. Qwen-full-prompt uses the original Event-STVG prompt, including the target ordinal, eventboundary definition, and all required roles, and returns the standard unified JSON. Qwen-PTD-style uses the same role-specific referring queries as PTD, queries each role independently, and returns simplified role-level bbox/tube JSON that is converted to the unified Event-STVG evaluation format. This adapts the PTD-style query/output interface without PTD-native decoding: Qwen generates no PTD special tokens. In both Qwen conditions, the original MP4 is sent through Qwens native video API with default generation settings; Qwen does not use PTDs 64-frame sampling. sections.title: D ADDITIONAL ERROR ANALYSIS
sections.content: We analyze Event-STVG failures along three recurrent paths: (1) event-instance confusion, where the model recognizes the event type but selects the wrong occurrence; (2) spatial role-grounding failure, where the target event is localized temporally but its role fillers are grounded poorly; and (3) incomplete multi-role composition, where only subset of the required roles is successfully localized. Together, these analyses cover both the soccer benchmark and the multidomain evaluation. Unless otherwise specified, results are reported in the order Gemini-3.7 Flash / GPT-5.6 Sol / Qwen-3.8 Max. D.1 EVENT-INSTANCE CONFUSION D.1.1 SOCCER Longer contexts substantially increase the difficulty of resolving the requested event occurrence. We focus on 209 soccer queries for which another qualified occurrence of the same event type appears in at least one context setting. From 1 to 10 minutes, target hit rates decrease by 43.54 / 21.05 / 44.98 percentage points, while same-type instance mismatch rates increase by 13.40 / 15.79 / 19.62 percentage points. All six changes remain significant after multiple-comparison correction. This degradation is driven primarily by losing the target occurrence rather than by progressively worse temporal boundaries once the target is found. Among queries successfully hit at all four durations, mean tIoU shows no consistent decline. For the 209-query group, the 1-to-10-minute changes are only 0.05 / +1.45 / 0.21 percentage points. This suggests that long contexts primarily challenge which occurrence to select, rather than boundary refinement after successful retrieval. Among queries hit at 1 minute but missed at 10 minutes, 26.04% / 55.36% / 38.61% overlap another qualified occurrence of the same type, providing further evidence that substantial fraction of long-context failures involve confusion with another plausible event instance. D.1.2 MULTIDOMAIN EVALUATION Instance-selection errors also occur beyond soccer. Among 500 multidomain queries, 106 / 104 / 88 predictions are more consistent with another annotated occurrence of the same event type than with the requested target under our candidate criterion. Such cases appear in all seven evaluated domains. Repeated events are particularly challenging in several sports domains. In basketball, mean tIoU decreases from 27.48 to 7.50, 37.57 to 16.79, and 27.79 to 14.20 when comparing the first three occurrences with the fourth or later occurrences. Over the same split, wrong-instance candidate rates increase from 23.33% to 42.98%, 16.67% to 39.52%, and 13.33% to 42.92%, respectively. Volleyball and ice hockey show similar reductions in later-occurrence tIoU, whereas daily work and entertainment do not exhibit the same consistent pattern. These results indicate that event-instance resolution is recurring difficulty across domains. However, the soccer duration experiment and the multidomain ordinal analysis capture different effects: later occurrences also covary with video position, event difficulty, and available visual evidence. D.2 TEMPORAL RETRIEVAL DOES NOT ENSURE SPATIAL ROLE GROUNDING Successfully locating an event in time does not imply that its participants are correctly grounded. In soccer, among temporally hit queries, mean GapSG remains high. At 1 minute, the gaps are 76.53% / 95.65% / 90.86%, and at 10 minutes they remain 77.25% / 97.01% / 96.77%. Restricting evaluation to queries jointly hit by all three models produces the same overall pattern. Across all four durations, Gemini exhibits significantly smaller spatial gap than GPT and Qwen on these matched queries. The phenomenon generalizes beyond soccer. On multidomain queries individually hit by each model, mean GapSG is 67.52% / 71.42% / 74.43%. When restricted to the same 206 queries jointly hit by all three models, the gaps remain 67.59% / 69.12% / 73.54%. The effect is especially pronounced in esports: on 30 jointly hit League of Legends queries, mean gaps reach 84.43% / 95.73% / 98.41%. 21 The same pattern remains under stronger temporal overlap. On the 26 multidomain multi-role queries for which all three models achieve tIoU > 0.5, mean gaps remain 78.13% / 91.07% / 88.08%. Therefore, temporal retrieval and spatial role grounding constitute distinct bottlenecks. model may identify when the requested event occurs while still failing to determine who fills its constituent semantic roles. D.3 INCOMPLETE MULTI-ROLE COMPOSITION Event-STVG further requires all queried role fillers to be grounded jointly, creating an additional compositional bottleneck beyond recovering individual participants. In soccer, we evaluate 179 queries requiring two or three roles. Even under the Oracle setting, where the ground-truth event interval is provided, only 40 / 6 / 7 queries achieve vIoU > 0.3 for every required role, corresponding to complete-success rates of 22.35% / 3.35% / 3.91%. By contrast, at least one role succeeds in 64.25% / 18.99% / 27.37% of the same queries. Thus, providing the correct temporal window does not remove the difficulty of assembling the complete event-role structure. The challenge is even more apparent in the multidomain set. Among 274 multi-role queries, at least one role is successfully localized in 20 / 6 / 9 cases, whereas all required roles succeed in only 4 / 2 / 0 cases. The corresponding complete-success rates are only 1.46% / 0.73% / 0.00%. None of the 52 three-role queries achieves complete success for any model. The gap persists after conditioning on strong temporal localization. Among the 26 multi-role queries jointly satisfying tIoU > 0.5, Gemini succeeds on at least one role in 10 cases but on all roles in only 2; GPT achieves 3 versus 2; and Qwen achieves 5 versus 0. These results show that recovering individual participants is not sufficient. Event-STVG requires models to compose all required role fillers into complete, spatially grounded event structure, which remains rare even when the event has already been localized in time. D.4 ROBUSTNESS CHECKS Several additional analyses confirm that the main observations are not artifacts of single diagnostic criterion. First, the increase in soccer instance mismatches remains significant under stricter definitions requiring overlap with another event interval or tIoU > 0.3 with the alternative occurrence. Second, among valid predictions that miss the target at 10 minutes, the observed rates of overlapping another same-type occurrence are 23.91% / 54.93% / 38.05%, compared with only 2.86% / 2.31% / 3.50% under random-position reference preserving prediction-window length. All three differences are significant after correction (p < 0.0001). The temporal degradation also remains when restricting soccer evaluation to queries with valid predicted time windows at every duration. From 1 to 10 minutes, hit rates still decrease by 43.27 / 21.05 / 44.10 percentage points, and mean tIoU decreases by 21.35 / 11.77 / 25.93 percentage points. Finally, the multi-role pattern is robust to the success threshold. Lowering the per-role criterion from vIoU > 0.3 to vIoU > 0.1 increases success rates, while raising it to vIoU > 0.5 decreases them, but complete role coverage remains substantially harder than partial coverage. D.5 INTERPRETATION The three error paths should be viewed as complementary diagnostics rather than independent probabilistic factors. Likewise, GapSG captures multiple sources of spatial error, including localization quality, role correspondence, visibility, missing predictions, and output validity, and should not be attributed to single internal mechanism. Taken together, the evidence reveals consistent cascade of difficulties: models must first resolve the requested occurrence among repeated events, then ground its semantic role fillers after temporal retrieval, and finally localize all required roles jointly. Failures arise at every stage, explaining why successful end-to-end Event-STVG remains difficult even for current frontier models. 22 DATASET CONSTRUCTION, ANNOTATION, AND QUALITY CONTROL This appendix provides additional details on the construction, annotation, and quality control of Event-STVG. We first describe the common annotation target and workflow, then detail the annotator-facing guidelines and domain-specific annotation procedures, and finally report the quality-control protocol and quantitative annotation audits. Evaluation metrics are provided in Appendix A, and prompt examples and the output format in Appendix B. E.1 ANNOTATION OVERVIEW Each Event-STVG instance is defined around specific event occurrence and contains three forms of ground truth: 1. the temporal interval of the event; 2. the semantic roles involved in the event; and 3. the spatial trajectory of the entity filling each role during the event. For long-context evaluation, occurrences of the same event type are additionally ordered within the model input to determine the target ordinal. Across all domains, annotation follows the same high-level workflow: 1. define the event semantics, temporal boundaries, required roles, and occurrence-counting rules; 2. identify the target occurrence and annotate its temporal boundaries; 3. annotate the entities filling the required semantic roles at approximately 2 FPS; 4. validate temporal, spatial, identity-consistency, and visibility annotations; 5. construct the final evaluation context and recompute the target ordinal within that context; and 6. generate the model query and corresponding ground truth from the frozen annotation. semantic role is defined by its relation to the target event rather than by the identity of the entity itself. For example, last passer refers to the player who directly passes to the shooter for the target shot, rather than to an arbitrary player who happens to make the last visible pass in the surrounding video. Within an event, the entity assigned to role must remain identity-consistent across frames. When role filler cannot be reliably localized in sampled frame, the spatial annotation is recorded as invisible rather than being assigned to another nearby entity. Throughout the construction pipeline, we retain mappings between the source video, source frames, timestamps, spatial coordinates, and the corresponding frames in the final model input. This distinction is important because, after cropping, concatenation, or re-encoding, the source-video timeline, the final-input timeline, and the nominal 2-FPS sampling timestamps need not coincide exactly. E.2 ANNOTATOR-FACING GUIDELINES To reduce annotation ambiguity, annotators follow task-specific operational guide that separates the annotation process into three stages: event-window annotation, role-trajectory annotation, and context/ordinal verification. Automatic timestamps, detections, and trajectories are treated only as annotation aids; final event boundaries, semantic-role assignments, role trajectories, occurrence sequences, and ordinals must be supported by the video itself. E.2.1 STAGE 1: EVENT-WINDOW ANNOTATION Annotators first verify that candidate clip contains the intended event. retained event must contain the correct event type and key action, be primarily observable in the standard broadcast view, and avoid unnecessary replay, close-up, or adjacent-event content. We do not apply universal temporal-boundary rule across event types. Instead, each event is annotated according to its semantic structure. Table E.1 summarizes the principal soccer rules exposed to annotators. Table E.1: Soccer event-specific roles and temporal-boundary guidelines. For shot events, the endpoint may correspond to goal, miss, goalkeeper save or control, defensive clearance, another player taking control, or broadcast cut. The last passer role is optional when no clear final pass exists. For card-related events, annotators label the foul that produces the card, rather than the later closeup of the referee displaying the card. For events requiring spatial event-location attribute, annotators record where the event itself occurs rather than where an earlier participant first receives possession. For example, shot is localized at the shooting location and foul at the contact location. E.2.2 STAGE 2: SEMANTIC-ROLE TRAJECTORY ANNOTATION Stage 2 begins from the temporal window finalized in Stage 1. Videos are sampled at approximately 2 FPS, and the interface provides automatically generated detections and player tracks without semantic-role assignments. Before assigning roles, annotators re-check that: the event type is correct; the key action is present; the event is primarily visible in the standard broadcast view; and the temporal window is not seriously shifted. 24 Minor boundary differences of few frames are not treated as failures when the event semantics, key action, broadcast view, and role structure remain intact. For each required semantic role, annotators follow four operations: Select. Assign the candidate player corresponding to the role. Inspect. Review the sampled frames to ensure that the trajectory continues to follow the same individual. Correct. Reassign role when the automatic track switches identity, drifts to another person, or otherwise becomes incorrect. Complete. Manually add bounding box when the role is clearly visible but no usable automatic detection exists, and remove incorrect boxes when necessary. stable track ID is not itself evidence of correct identity. Conversely, change in track ID does not imply that the role filler has changed. Semantic identity is determined from the event and the visual evidence. Annotators draw box only when the role filler is visible and can be reliably identified. They do not infer location while the person is occluded or outside the frame. Optional roles, such as last passer, remain absent when no reliable role filler exists. E.2.3 CONTEXT AND ORDINAL VERIFICATION After temporal and role annotations are finalized, the target event is placed into longer evaluation context. For each query, annotators or reviewers: 1. identify all occurrences in the context that satisfy the query-specific event definition; 2. order them chronologically; 3. locate the target event in that sequence; and 4. assign its ordinal. The target is the first occurrence if no qualifying event precedes it and the n-th occurrence if exactly 1 qualifying events appear earlier. Occurrence counting follows the query definition, rather than simply counting all available source labels. single real-world event can belong to several semantic categories. For example, direct free kick that scores may also qualify as shot on target and goal. Such an event is counted once within each query-specific occurrence sequence, while its ordinal is computed separately for each sequence. Similarly, different foul queries define different occurrence sets. query for the n-th foul leading to penalty counts different subset from query for the n-th foul in general. Not every source occurrence must correspond to retained Event-STVG target annotation. source event may be excluded as target because it is insufficiently visible, lacks the required key action, or fails manual review. However, if it remains valid occurrence under the current query definition and can be verified in the video, it may still contribute to the occurrence sequence used for ordinal assignment. E.2.4 FINAL ANNOTATOR VERIFICATION After the context and ordinal are generated, the final sample is manually reviewed. sample is marked Pass only when: the target event is correctly mapped; the target event is complete; the query-specific occurrence set is correct; there are no missing, duplicated, or incorrectly counted occurrences; and the target ordinal is correct. If any of these conditions fails, the sample is marked Fail. The resulting end-to-end workflow is: 25 candidate retrieval event verification and temporal annotation event attributes automatic detection/tracking manual semantic-role assignment frame-level trajectory correction final event/role confirmation context construction occurrence and ordinal generation manual final verification dataset finalization. The central annotation principle is that automatic outputs are treated as suggestions, while the final Event-STVG ground truth must be supported by evidence that can be directly verified from the video. E.3 SOCCER ANNOTATION E.3.1 TEMPORAL ANNOTATION For soccer, we first use existing event annotations to retrieve candidate occurrences from full broadcast matches. These annotations are used only for candidate retrieval and occurrence association and are not directly adopted as the final temporal intervals. Annotators inspect the surrounding video and manually determine the start and end of each event according to the event-specific rules above. Unrelated replays, celebrations, close-ups, and subsequent phases of play are excluded when applicable. Some source events are further decomposed according to the event semantics used in Event-STVG. For example, the action that results in corner and the subsequent corner kick are treated as separate events. Likewise, foul leading to free kick and the execution of the free kick are annotated independently. The resulting temporal interval therefore corresponds to the semantics of the EventSTVG event rather than directly inheriting point timestamp from the source annotation. We additionally audit the mapping from locally annotated candidate clips back to the full-match timeline. All 3,516 soccer targets in the final benchmark have valid temporal mappings. E.3.2 SPATIAL ROLE ANNOTATION After temporal annotation, candidate player trajectories are generated using SoccerMaster DETR, PRTReID, and StrongSORT. These trajectories serve only as annotation assistance and do not directly constitute ground truth. Annotators identify the players corresponding to the semantic roles from the event context and inspect candidate trajectories at approximately 2 FPS. They retain full control over the trajectories, including reassigning tracks, removing erroneous detections, resolving track-ID switches, and manually adding missing boxes. When role filler cannot be reliably localized in sampled frame, that frame is marked as invisible. For 25-FPS source videos, half-second sampling is realized by rounding the corresponding frame positions, e.g., 0, 13, 25, 38, 50, ... rather than by sampling at fixed 12-frame interval, which would introduce accumulated temporal drift. All ground-truth boxes are first retained in the original image coordinate system together with their source-frame identities and are transformed only when adapting them to the final model input. E.3.3 CONTEXT CONSTRUCTION AND ORDINAL ASSIGNMENT After the target events are frozen, we construct the Oracle and 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-minute evaluation settings. The same target events and semantic roles are retained across context durations. Each target interval is mapped into the corresponding context, while qualified same-type occurrences are deduplicated and temporally ordered to determine the ordinal of the target within that context. Consequently, the underlying target event remains unchanged across durations, while its ordinal index may change as the context expands. E.4 MULTIDOMAIN ANNOTATION The multidomain evaluation set contains 500 target events organized into 100 final evaluation videos. 26 We retain the same eventrole annotation abstraction across domains, while adapting the annotation interface to the form of the available source data. Depending on the domain, annotators either draw boxes directly on original frames, select from existing tracking trajectories, or annotate against frame-exact JPEG sequences. Table E.2: Event types and semantic roles in the multidomain evaluation. E.4.1 SPORTS DOMAINS Basketball Shot events are annotated on the original possession clips. By default, the event begins with the direct pass to the shooter and ends when the shot, layup, or dunk is completed. Spatial annotations for the last passer and shooter are mapped to the nearest real source frame at each nominal half-second sampling point. For ice hockey, annotators first define the temporal interval of the Shot and then assign semantic roles using existing player trajectories as candidates. Selecting candidate initializes the corresponding role tube, after which the complete trajectory is reviewed for identity switches, box drift, and incorrectly missing frames. For volleyball, annotations are performed against the original 25-FPS JPEG frames. rally may contain multiple independently annotated Serve or Spike events, including temporally overlapping event windows when semantically appropriate. For Spike events, the blocker role is additionally annotated when reliable spatial evidence is available. E.4.2 ESPORTS, ANIMAL ACTIVITY, AND DAILY SCENARIOS For League of Legends, Kill event covers the combat leading to the target death. The killer and victim must be localized in the main game view rather than through minimap icons, portraits, kill notifications, or player-camera overlays. When multiple kills occur within the same fight, occurrence order is determined by victim death time. Animal annotations distinguish the Initial Attack stage from the Final Subdual stage of hunt. Each event grounds the predator and prey, while the predator responsible for the initial attack need not be the same individual as the one responsible for the final subdual. For Food Packaging, the spatial target is the food together with its active packaging rather than the worker performing the action. The temporal interval focuses on packaging and closure and excludes food preparation and subsequent transportation after packaging is complete. For The Voice, each Turn event grounds the mentor performing the chair turn. Multiple turns within the same performance are ordered temporally. E.5 QUALITY-CONTROL PROTOCOL Event-STVG uses multiple levels of quality control because structurally valid annotations may still be semantically incorrect. E.5.1 STRUCTURAL VALIDATION We first perform automatic checks to verify that: 27 annotation files are parseable; sample identifiers are unique; temporal boundaries are correctly ordered and lie within the source media; sampled frame indices are valid, ordered, and non-duplicated; bounding boxes have positive area and lie within the corresponding image coordinate system; frozen annotations contain no stale or unfinished spatial records; and frozen annotations, final-video manifests, query specifications, and ground-truth files are mutually consistent. E.5.2 TEMPORAL AND MEDIA ALIGNMENT For all constructed videos, source-frame provenance is retained through cropping, concatenation, resizing, padding, and re-encoding. Event boundaries and sampled role frames are mapped to actual output frames or timestamps rather than being inferred solely from nominal frame rates. We explicitly distinguish three notions of time: the annotation time in the source video; the mapped time in the final input video; and the nominal half-second sampling time. This prevents re-encoding or frame-rate conversion from silently changing the visual evidence referenced by the annotation. E.5.3 SEMANTIC HUMAN REVIEW Automatic validation can verify that box is structurally valid, but it cannot establish that the box contains the correct semantic role filler. Human review therefore checks whether: the target event actually occurs; the temporal boundaries follow the event definition; each selected entity satisfies the required semantic role; role identity remains consistent throughout the event; invisible annotations correspond to genuinely unlocalizable frames rather than missed boxes; and annotation guidelines, interface instructions, and final query text are semantically consistent. E.5.4 OCCURRENCE AND ORDINAL VALIDATION Ordinal grounding introduces an additional source of annotation error. Even if the temporal interval and role trajectories of an event are correct, the corresponding query is still incorrect if the event is assigned the wrong occurrence number. We therefore separately verify same-type occurrences and their temporal ordering when constructing the final evaluation contexts. Replay or duplicate representations of the same physical event are not intended to create new occurrences. E.5.5 CROSS-REVIEW AND END-TO-END HUMAN AUDIT For soccer, we additionally conduct paired re-annotation: 355 samples for temporal annotation; and 355 samples for spatial role annotation. The temporal review interface displays the original interval as read-only reference, while the role review uses the same tracking candidates as the original annotation. We therefore interpret this experiment as measuring annotation consistency under the current interface and workflow rather than as independent double-blind annotation. 28 In addition, we perform final human audit of the multidomain evaluation set. We sample 50 cases from the 500 multidomain instances according to the scene distribution and manually inspect each frozen benchmark instance as whole. This audit does not involve redrawing bounding boxes or re-annotating temporal boundaries. Instead, annotators directly judge whether the existing annotation and final query are jointly correct with respect to three components: 1. temporal localization of the target event; 2. spatial localization of the required semantic roles; and 3. the occurrence ordinal of the target event in the final video. Each sampled instance receives binary Pass/Fail judgment and is considered Pass only when all three components are correct. E.6 ANNOTATION AGREEMENT AND FINAL AUDITS The paired soccer annotation results are summarized below. Table E.3: Soccer paired-annotation agreement. Among roleframe pairs for which both annotations contain visible box, the mean bounding-box IoU is 0.945. When one-sided missing boxes are additionally included and assigned zero overlap, the mean decreases to 0.919, with 2.70% of roleframe pairs containing box on only one side. We report both quantities because evaluating only jointly visible frames would obscure disagreements in visibility annotation. Beyond paired annotation, we conduct several construction-level audits. For soccer, the final temporal-correction manifest contains all 3,516 unique target events, each with valid temporal mapping. We additionally perform fixed final review of 176 targets across the constructed temporal settings, and all 176 pass the final review. The Oracle and 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-minute manifests each contain the same set of 3,516 target IDs, providing an additional consistency check that context construction does not change the evaluated target set. For the multidomain data, the frozen release contains: 500 target events; 100 final input videos; 6,639 role-sampling records; 5,777 visible bounding-box annotations; and 862 invisible records. No frozen target contains stale spatial annotation. If role contains no valid spatial evidence over the entire event, that role is omitted from the corresponding final model query while its original annotation is retained in the provenance. Roles that are invisible only in subset of frames remain part of the query. On top of these construction checks, we sample 50 instances from the 500 multidomain cases according to the scene distribution and perform an end-to-end human quality audit. Each instance is evaluated with binary Pass/Fail criterion that jointly considers temporal localization, spatial role localization, and the correctness of the target occurrence ordinal. All 50 sampled instances pass the audit, corresponding to sample-level pass rate of 100%. This audit is complementary to the paired annotation study above. It does not re-estimate temporal or spatial annotations and therefore is not used to measure inter-annotator tIoU or bounding-box IoU. Instead, it directly verifies whether frozen benchmark instance remains jointly correct in temporal localization, spatial grounding, and ordinal assignment under the final video and query presented to the model. We also audit the multidomain media-construction pipeline by decoding the final videos and checking the mapping between annotated source frames and output frames. According to the recorded construction audits, the maximum source-to-output temporal mapping discrepancy is approximately 0.017 s. Finally, we run regression tests covering: role filtering; occurrence handling; ordinal assignment; sampling provenance; coordinate transformation; and query/ground-truth formatting. These checks address complementary failure modes. Automatic validation establishes structural and media-mapping consistency; paired re-annotation measures temporal and spatial consistency under the annotation workflow; annotator-facing operational rules constrain how temporal boundaries, semantic roles, and occurrence sequences are defined; and the final end-to-end human audit directly evaluates whether frozen instances are jointly correct in temporal localization, spatial localization, and occurrence ordinal. We therefore report structural consistency, annotation agreement, operational annotation guidelines, and final sample-level human audit as complementary forms of quality evidence rather than treating any single check as equivalent to complete independent re-annotation.
